hook: Africa's rarest carnivore lives on islands in the sky.

story.text: The Ethiopian wolf is a wolf in fox's clothing: bright tawny-rufous with white markings, long slender legs, a fine narrow muzzle.
It lives only on the roof of Africa — mountain meadows between 3,000 and 4,500 meters, on islands of sky too far apart to cross.
It is Africa's rarest carnivore: fewer than five hundred adults, in six separated populations.
Its habits are split in two: packs greet and patrol together at dawn and dusk, but every wolf hunts alone.
The prey is rodents — above all the giant molerat, an Afroalpine animal found nowhere else.
The killer arrives on four familiar feet: rabies and distemper spill over from village dogs, crashing whole populations in weeks.
The response is a vaccine hidden inside a piece of meat, left in the field where a wolf will find it.
The program vaccinates the dogs too — more than three thousand a year around wolf country.
Meanwhile the mountains themselves shrink: sixty percent of wolf range has already gone under barley and potatoes.
To witness the Ethiopian wolf is to stand with the monitors who log thousands of sightings a year, holding a species steady one pack at a time.

reproduction.text: Only the pack's alpha female breeds. Up to seven pups emerge from the den at three weeks, born between October and December, and the whole pack rears them — delivering prey and regurgitating meals.

insight.text: Ethiopian wolves are solitary hunters but social sleepers — the pack patrols its borders together at dawn and rests together at night, yet every hunt is made alone.

programs.title: One Health vaccination
programs.summary: Oral rabies vaccines hidden in meat for wolves, and over 3,000 village dogs vaccinated each year to stop spillover at its source.
